content: Between 2012 and October 17, 2022, a total of 2,600 laboratory-confirmed cases of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (MERS-CoV) infection were reported to the World Health Organization (WHO). Of these, 84% (2,193 cases) were reported by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. MERS cases have been documented in 27 countries across the Middle East, North Africa, Europe, the United States, and Asia. To date, 935 deaths have been attributed to MERS, resulting in a crude case fatality rate of 36%. The majority of cases (69%) were male, with a median age of 58 years (interquartile range: 44–70 years, range: 23–98 years). Three additional cases from 2017 were retrospectively reported to WHO from Qatar, including one fatality. Since the last update, approximately 81% of cases (120 out of 148) reported at least one underlying condition, such as chronic renal failure, heart disease, diabetes mellitus, or hypertension. Among the 148 cases detected since July 2019, 8 (5%) were asymptomatic or had mild disease. This proportion is lower than the 22% of cases reported as asymptomatic or mild in the previous global summary from July 2019. This reduction likely reflects decreased testing and case detection due to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, rather than a change in the virulence of the virus. The epidemiology, transmission patterns, clinical presentation, and viral characteristics of MERS-CoV remain consistent with previous patterns described in earlier WHO global summaries. MERS-CoV is a zoonotic virus that has repeatedly entered the human population through direct or indirect contact with infected dromedary camels in the Arabian Peninsula. Human-to-human transmission has occurred among close contacts and in healthcare settings, but outside of healthcare environments, human-to-human transmission has been limited. Preventive measures such as mask-wearing, hand hygiene, physical distancing, improved indoor ventilation, and respiratory etiquette have likely reduced opportunities for onward human-to-human transmission of MERS-CoV. However, the circulation of MERS-CoV in dromedary camels is unlikely to have been affected by measures introduced to limit SARS-CoV-2 transmission. While the number of reported secondary cases of MERS has decreased, the risk of zoonotic transmission remains. WHO anticipates additional cases of MERS-CoV infection will be reported from the Middle East, particularly as epidemiological surveillance activities resume. Cases may also continue to be exported to other countries by individuals exposed to dromedaries, animal products (e.g., raw camel milk), or infected humans (e.g., in healthcare settings). Early identification of cases in the community and healthcare systems, increasing public awareness about MERS-CoV and its prevention, adherence to infection prevention and control measures, and contact follow-up remain critical priorities for MERS outbreak prevention and control. Recent clusters of MERS-CoV infections have been reported, including household and nosocomial clusters in Saudi Arabia and Qatar. These clusters highlight the importance of infection prevention and control measures in healthcare settings to prevent human-to-human transmission. Zoonotic transmission of MERS-CoV continues to be a concern. Improvements in multi-sectoral investigations of community-acquired cases have been observed, including testing of dromedary camels and follow-up of human contacts of confirmed cases. Ministries of Health in affected countries notify Ministries of Agriculture when human cases report exposure to dromedary camels through occupational, recreational, or other contact. Investigations in dromedaries are conducted by agricultural officials, and positive results are reported to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH). Human-to-human transmission of MERS-CoV remains limited, with most transmission occurring in healthcare facilities. This remains a prominent feature of MERS-CoV epidemiology. WHO continues to collaborate with health authorities in affected countries to prevent and minimize healthcare-associated cases and improve infection prevention and control measures in healthcare facilities. Despite these efforts, MERS remains a relatively rare disease, and awareness among healthcare personnel, even in the Middle East, is generally low. The non-specific symptoms of MERS-CoV infection, ranging from no symptoms to pneumonia and acute respiratory distress syndrome, can lead to missed diagnoses, particularly in cases presenting with mild respiratory symptoms. The exact drivers and modes of transmission in healthcare settings are not well-defined and remain the focus of active research. Observational studies suggest that transmission in healthcare settings often occurs before adequate infection prevention and control procedures are implemented and before cases are isolated. Aerosol-generating procedures conducted in crowded emergency departments or medical wards with suboptimal infection control measures have been implicated in human-to-human transmission and environmental contamination. Improved compliance with infection prevention and control measures can reduce and potentially eliminate human-to-human transmission in healthcare facilities. Globally, the median age of MERS cases is 53 years (interquartile range: 38–66 years), and 69% of cases are male. Approximately 20% of cases had no or mild symptoms, while 48% had severe disease or died. Over 70% of fatal cases had at least one underlying condition, such as diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, chronic renal failure, or lung disease. Since 2012, 27 countries have reported MERS-CoV cases, with the majority (84%) reported from Saudi Arabia. Healthcare workers account for at least 17% of all reported cases. The largest outbreak outside the Middle East occurred in South Korea in 2015, resulting in 186 cases and 39 deaths. Early suspicion, isolation, and contact tracing were critical in preventing further transmission during a subsequent exported case to South Korea in 2018. The basic reproduction number (R0) of MERS-CoV is generally less than 1, with significant variability in specific contexts. In healthcare settings, the R0 can exceed 1, but outbreaks can be controlled with proper infection prevention and control measures and early isolation of cases. The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted many MERS-related activities, but the WHO Global Program of Work for MERS-CoV has informed the response to COVID-19. Expert networks, reference laboratories, technical guidance, and standardized protocols developed for MERS-CoV were rapidly adapted for COVID-19, providing a foundation for early and informed actions by WHO and Member States. Recent WHO activities include technical missions to Saudi Arabia, the designation of a WHO Collaborating Centre for MERS, and virtual meetings to review the MERS situation in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic.
